Routing evidence:

- C was accepted once: REQ-2409, a large invoice from the east region, submitted by Sam Haddad (Field Sales), with note “Second attempt, the first form bounced.”
- Identical core attributes (large invoice, east region) produced both rejection (REQ-2401) and acceptance (REQ-2409), so size/type/region alone do not determine the route. Requester context or note may matter.
- No evidence yet distinguishes options A, B, or D. Avoid assuming C is correct; seek more examples or use the full ticket context.

Routing evidence:
- Option C (regional office) was rejected in 12 of 13 observed requests; do not select it merely because the requester mentions a regional office, east region, a large request, or “Second attempt, the first form bounced.”
- C was accepted only for REQ-2409: a large east-region invoice from Sam Haddad (Field Sales), with “Second attempt, the first form bounced.” Similar attributes were rejected for REQ-2401, REQ-2416 (large east claim), and REQ-2419 (small east invoice), so requester identity/full context likely matters.
- Option A (standard queue) was accepted for REQ-2414 (large north refund, Field Sales; “Let me know if anything is missing”), REQ-2417 (small north refund, Regional Ops; “Same as the ones I sent last month”), and REQ-2418 (small south shipment, Field Sales; “Let me know if anything is missing”).
- A was rejected for REQ-2411 (small east claim, Client Services; “Same as the ones I sent last month”). Thus note text alone does not determine routing, though A currently has the strongest positive evidence.
- Recent tests: B was rejected for REQ-2410 and REQ-2413; D was rejected for REQ-2412. These are only individual cases and do not establish general rules.
- Do not infer routes from size, type, region, department, or note alone. Use the closest accepted precedent, especially requester/context combinations; otherwise seek more evidence and avoid assuming C, B, or D.

Do not choose C merely because the note mentions a regional office.
